13	
14	You produce a report on agent behavior during experiments: how many
15	trials per hour, where the loop stalled, attempts to terminate early,
16	and how stable the metrics are across multiple runs of the same
17	configuration.
18	
19	## Modes
20	
21	- **Single-experiment mode** — when `tag=` selects exactly one
22	  experiment, the cross-branch variance metrics collapse. Drop the
23	  `mean` / `stddev` summary row and call out the small sample size in
24	  the executive summary.
25	- **Multi-experiment mode** — every other case. Variance across runs
26	  is the headline signal.
27	
28	## Arguments
29	
30	- `tag=<tag>[,<tag>...]` — restrict to specific experiments by their
31	  run tags. Omitting `tag=` defaults to a report across every
32	  experiment under `refs/heads/autocuda/optimize/`.
33	- `output=<name>` — report output name. Default: the selected tag when
34	  exactly one `tag=` is given, otherwise `<timestamp>-consolidated`.
35	
36	## Procedure
37	
38	1. **Build the data CSV.** Run
39	
40	   ```
41	   eval "$(autocuda report data behavior \
42	       [--tag <experiment-tag> ...] \
43	       [--output <output>])"
44	   ```
45	
46	   `eval` captures the `OUTPUT="<name>"` line the CLI prints on stdout. The CSV is written to
47	   `<data-dir>/<OUTPUT>-report-behavior.csv` with one row per branch:
48	   `trials`, `duration_seconds`, `trials_per_hour`, `gap_count`
49	   (transitions > 10min between trials), `max_gap_seconds`,
50	   `improvement_pct_total` (best `pct_change` recorded on a kept row
51	   — `improved` for single-file skills; tree-worker logs don't carry
52	   `pct_change`, so this column is `+0.00` for tree branches).
53	
54	2. **Sanity-check the data schema.** Run
55	   `autocuda schema check report-behavior-csv --output "$OUTPUT"`.
56	
57	3. **For `/autocuda:optimize-tree` runs only, surface fleet behavior.** If any selected branch is shaped `autocuda/optimize/<MGR>/{worker-N,worker-N-brief-R,manager-combine}` (i.e. the run was a tree-search rather than a single-line `optimize-simple`), add a dedicated **"Fleet Behavior"** markdown section that covers:
58	
59	   - **Worker concurrency over time.** Read every `<MGR>-optimize-tree-worker-<N>-log.csv`, pair each worker's `brief_start` and `brief_stop` rows, bucket the active intervals into 5-minute windows, and count distinct active workers per window. 60	   - **Brief-cycle timing.** For each row in `<MGR>-optimize-tree-manager-log.csv` (every row is a brief), find the first non-lifecycle row in `<MGR>-optimize-tree-worker-<agent_id>-log.csv` whose timestamp postdates the brief. 61	   - **Lock contention.** Grep the session JSONLs (see step 4) for paired `[autocuda run] acquired lock=<name> mode=<exclusive|shared> at=<iso> wait=<s>` and `[autocuda run] released lock=<name> mode=<exclusive|shared> at=<iso> ran=<s>` lines — `autocuda run slice` and `autocuda run exclusive` emit both on every invocation. The lock name is `build` for slices (which take a shared lock on every GPU) and `gpu-<g>` for an exclusive on the GPU `g` it claimed (chosen dynamically — a benchmark's `wait` includes any time all GPUs were busy). Match them by lock + time order to get per-call wait + run durations. Aggregate by `lock` name (per-GPU load falls out of the `gpu-<g>` split), by `mode` (shared = `slice` = builds; exclusive = bench / profile / validate), and by `agent_id` (each JSONL maps to one worker). Report total wait per lock kind, the worst single wait, and the worker that paid the most. If aggregate lock-wait is a meaningful fraction of fleet walltime, say so explicitly.
62	   - **Per-worker reliability.** Aggregate the Throughput rows by worker id parsed from the branch leaf (`worker-N` or `worker-N-brief-R`). Use this section to call out outliers: any worker whose trials-per-hour is more than 2× off the fleet median.
63	
64	   Skip this section entirely for single-process `optimize-simple` runs (no `/worker-` segment in any selected branch). When you include it, place it in the markdown right after the executive summary so it's visible without scrolling.
65	
66	4. **Surface aberrant behavior the CSV cannot capture.** The CLI only
67	   sees the log; the agent harness records have richer signal. For
68	   each branch in scope, find the most recent session JSONL whose
69	   first timestamp falls within the branch's first/last log timestamps
70	   and read it. Don't ask the user to confirm — proceed with the best
71	   automatic match. If the user explicitly passed JSONL paths in the
72	   conversation, use those instead. Look for:
73	   - **Early-termination attempts.** Any "should I keep going?" /
74	     "experiment has converged" / "done" outputs. Count them per
75	     branch; record the trial number where they appeared.
76	   - **Unexplained gaps.** Map every `gap_count` from the CSV back to
77	     the harness log to explain it (waiting on a slow benchmark? a
78	     compaction? the agent went silent?).
79	   - **Schema/log violations.** The agent edited the CSV by hand,
80	     skipped a row, or fabricated a timestamp.
81	
82	5. **Write the markdown report** to `<data-dir>/<OUTPUT>-report-behavior.md`. The markdown schema (enforced in step 6) requires these `##` sections, in order:
83	
84	   ### Executive Summary
85	   Lead with a 2–3 sentence high-level read on the run: was it
86	   productive (mean trials/hour), reliable (gap count, early-term
87	   attempts), and stable across branches (variance)? Then a
88	   **Key takeaways** sub-block of 3–5 bullets — the headlines a
89	   reader should walk away with even if they read nothing else.
90	   Examples: *"Worker 3 spent 42% of its walltime blocked on the
91	   exclusive lock"*, *"Cross-branch trials/hour variance is 0.18× —
92	   the runs are very consistent"*, *"Two branches contain
93	   early-termination attempts the agent recovered from"*. Then
94	   the existing one-line: branch count, total trials, total
95	   walltime, mean and worst-case trials/hour, overall reliability
96	   verdict. The detail sections below progressively disclose; the
97	   reader who only reads this section should still have the story.
98	
99	   ### Fleet Behavior (Optimize-Tree Runs Only)
100	   The four sub-sections from step 4 — worker concurrency, brief-cycle
101	   timing, lock contention, per-worker reliability — combined into one
102	   `##` block, in that order. Each sub-section is a short `###`
103	   header. Omit the whole block (header included) for
104	   `optimize-simple` runs; the markdown schema treats it as optional.
105	
106	   ### Throughput
107	   A table with columns, in order: Branch · Trials · Duration ·
108	   Trials/hour · Improvement %. Sorted by trials/hour descending.
109	   In multi-experiment mode, add a final row for the cross-branch
110	   `mean` and `stddev` of trials/hour and improvement % — this is the
111	   variance signal the user asked for.
112	
113	   ### Gaps And Stalls
114	   For each branch with `gap_count > 0`, a short paragraph: how many
115	   gaps, longest gap duration, plausible cause from the harness log.
116	   Skip branches with `gap_count = 0`.
117	
118	   ### Early-Termination Attempts
119	   Per-branch counts of the patterns from step 5 above. If none, say
120	   so in one line and skip the section's body.
121	
122	   ### Other Aberrant Behavior
123	   A bulleted list of anything noteworthy that none of the above
124	   sections cover (e.g. agent re-read the same file 50 times,
125	   skipped logging a trial). One bullet per incident; cite branch and
126	   trial number.
127	
128	   ### Analysis
129	   2–4 short paragraphs of narrative that ties the tables together.
130	   What does the data mean? Where did time actually go? Were the
131	   gaps caused by long benchmarks, lock contention, or agent stalls
132	   — and which is the bottleneck on the next run? Was variance
133	   driven by one outlier branch or distributed across the fleet?
134	   This section is the *why*, not the *what*; the tables above
135	   already cover *what*. Cite specific branches and trial numbers
136	   when making claims. Close with a one-paragraph "Recommendations"
137	   that lists the 2–3 concrete next steps the data supports.
138	
139	6. **Sanity-check the markdown structure.** Run
140	   `autocuda schema check report-behavior-markdown --output "$OUTPUT"`. If it
141	   fails, fix the report — don't ship it.
142	
143	7. **Convert to HTML.** `autocuda report html <data-dir>/$OUTPUT-report-behavior.md`. This writes `<data-dir>/<OUTPUT>-report-behavior.html` and requires pandoc on PATH.
144	
145	8. **Print a brief summary to stdout:** branch count, mean trials/hour,
146	   total early-termination attempts, top issue. For optimize-tree runs, also surface peak worker concurrency and aggregate lock-wait.
147	
148	## Constraints
149	
150	- **Be concise; don't repeat yourself; cut redundancy.** Each section should carry information the others do not. If you catch yourself rephrasing what is already above, delete the duplicate; if the report restates context the reader already has, edit it down.
151	- **Don't rewrite history.** This skill produces a report; it does not
152	  rewrite, revert, or push experiment branches.

import csv, datetime as dt, statistics, os, glob, re

DATA="/home/shadeform/gpumode/autocuda"
TAG="2026-06-22-09-10-03-qr_v2"
WLOG=lambda w: f"{DATA}/{TAG}-optimize-tree-worker-{w}-log.csv"
MLOG=f"{DATA}/{TAG}-optimize-tree-manager-log.csv"

def parse(ts):
    return dt.datetime.fromisoformat(ts)

# ---------- Load worker logs ----------
workers=[0,1,2,3]
wrows={}  # w -> list of dict rows
for w in workers:
    rows=[]
    with open(WLOG(w)) as f:
        r=csv.reader(f)
        header=next(r)
        for line in r:
            if len(line)<6:
                continue
            # cols: timestamp,agent_id,brief_id,iteration,linalg/qr_v2,status,commit,description
            try:
                ts=parse(line[0])
            except Exception:
                continue
            rows.append({'ts':ts,'agent_id':line[1],'brief_id':line[2],
                         'iter':line[3],'status':line[5] if len(line)>5 else '',
                         'commit':line[6] if len(line)>6 else ''})
    wrows[w]=rows

# ---------- Run span ----------
all_ts=[r['ts'] for w in workers for r in wrows[w]]
run_start=min(all_ts); run_end=max(all_ts)
print("RUN SPAN:", run_start, "->", run_end, " =", (run_end-run_start).total_seconds()/3600,"h")

# ---------- Per-worker first/last activity ----------
print("\n=== PER-WORKER FIRST/LAST ===")
wspan={}
for w in workers:
    ts=[r['ts'] for r in wrows[w]]
    wspan[w]=(min(ts),max(ts))
    print(f"W{w}: {min(ts)} -> {max(ts)}  ({(max(ts)-min(ts)).total_seconds()/3600:.2f}h)")

# ---------- Build active intervals from brief_start/brief_stop ----------
# Pair each brief_start with the NEXT brief_stop in time order for that worker.
print("\n=== INTERVAL PAIRING (brief_start -> next brief_stop) ===")
intervals={}  # w -> list of (start,stop)
unpaired_starts={}
extra_stops={}
for w in workers:
    rows=sorted(wrows[w], key=lambda r:r['ts'])
    starts=[r for r in rows if r['status']=='brief_start']
    stops =[r for r in rows if r['status']=='brief_stop']
    # greedy pairing in time order
    ivs=[]
    stop_q=sorted(stops,key=lambda r:r['ts'])
    used=[False]*len(stop_q)
    n_unpaired=0
    for s in starts:
        # find first stop after s not used
        found=False
        for i,st in enumerate(stop_q):
            if not used[i] and st['ts']>=s['ts']:
                ivs.append((s['ts'],st['ts'],s['brief_id']))
                used[i]=True
                found=True
                break
        if not found:
            # open interval -> close at worker last activity
            ivs.append((s['ts'],wspan[w][1],s['brief_id']))
            n_unpaired+=1
    intervals[w]=ivs
    unpaired_starts[w]=n_unpaired
    extra_stops[w]=sum(1 for u in used if not u)
    print(f"W{w}: {len(starts)} starts, {len(stops)} stops, {len(ivs)} intervals, "
          f"{n_unpaired} starts left open (closed at last activity), "
          f"{extra_stops[w]} unmatched stops (manager bookkeeping/balancing)")

# ---------- Worker concurrency: bucket into 5-min windows ----------
print("\n=== CONCURRENCY (5-min windows) ===")
BUCKET=300
def floor_bucket(t):
    epoch=int((t-run_start).total_seconds())
    return epoch - (epoch % BUCKET)

# total buckets across run
total_secs=(run_end-run_start).total_seconds()
nbuck=int(total_secs//BUCKET)+1
active_count=[0]*nbuck  # distinct active workers per bucket
# track which workers active in each bucket
bucket_workers=[set() for _ in range(nbuck)]
for w in workers:
    for (s,e,bid) in intervals[w]:
        b0=floor_bucket(s)//BUCKET
        b1=floor_bucket(e)//BUCKET

    active_count[b]=len(bucket_workers[b])

from collections import Counter
dist=Counter(active_count)
print("Buckets by #active workers:", dict(sorted(dist.items())))
peak=max(active_count)
print("Peak concurrency:", peak)
# time at each level
for lvl in range(0,5):
    cnt=sum(1 for a in active_count if a==lvl)
    print(f"  exactly {lvl} active: {cnt} buckets = {cnt*BUCKET/3600:.2f}h ({100*cnt/nbuck:.1f}%)")
# time at >= desired (4) and below
desired=4
at_or_above=sum(1 for a in active_count if a>=desired)
below=sum(1 for a in active_count if a<desired and a>0)
zero=sum(1 for a in active_count if a==0)
print(f"At full strength (>= {desired}): {at_or_above} buckets = {at_or_above*BUCKET/3600:.2f}h ({100*at_or_above/nbuck:.1f}%)")
print(f"Under strength (1..{desired-1}): {below} buckets = {below*BUCKET/3600:.2f}h ({100*below/nbuck:.1f}%)")
print(f"Fully idle (0 active): {zero} buckets = {zero*BUCKET/3600:.2f}h ({100*zero/nbuck:.1f}%)")

# longest under-strength stretch (treating 4 as target, but note W3 absent first ~1.6d)
def longest_run(pred):
    best=0; cur=0; best_start=None; cur_start=None
    for b in range(nbuck):

            if cur==0: cur_start=b
            cur+=1
            if cur>best:
                best=cur; best_start=cur_start
        else:
            cur=0
    return best, best_start
lb,lstart=longest_run(lambda a: a<4 and a>0)
print(f"Longest under-strength (1..3) stretch: {lb} buckets = {lb*BUCKET/3600:.2f}h starting bucket {lstart} (~{run_start+dt.timedelta(seconds=lstart*BUCKET) if lstart is not None else 'NA'})")

# Concurrency considering only the 3-worker era (before W3) vs 4-worker era
w3_first=wspan[3][0]
print(f"\nW3 first activity: {w3_first}  (so target was 3 before this, 4 after)")
# Era split
def era_stats(label, lo, hi, target):
    b0=int((lo-run_start).total_seconds())//BUCKET
    b1=int((hi-run_start).total_seconds())//BUCKET
    seg=active_count[b0:b1+1]
    n=len(seg)
    full=sum(1 for a in seg if a>=target)
    under=sum(1 for a in seg if 0<a<target)
    idle=sum(1 for a in seg if a==0)
    print(f"  {label}: {n} buckets ({n*BUCKET/3600:.2f}h), target={target}; "
          f"full {full} ({100*full/n:.1f}%), under {under} ({100*under/n:.1f}%), idle {idle} ({100*idle/n:.1f}%)")
print("\n=== ERA-AWARE CONCURRENCY ===")
era_stats("3-worker era (start->W3 spawn)", run_start, w3_first, 3)
era_stats("4-worker era (W3 spawn->end)", w3_first, run_end, 4)

# ---------- Trials (succeeded rows) per worker & per brief ----------
print("\n=== TRIALS (succeeded rows) ===")
wtrials=Counter()
for w in workers:
    for r in wrows[w]:
        if r['status']=='succeeded':
            wtrials[w]+=1
for w in workers:
    print(f"W{w}: {wtrials[w]} succeeded trials")
print("Total succeeded:", sum(wtrials.values()))

# ---------- Brief-cycle / handoff latency ----------
# For each manager-log row (a brief), find first non-lifecycle worker row whose ts postdates the brief.
print("\n=== HANDOFF LATENCY (manager brief row -> first worker activity) ===")
mrows=[]
with open(MLOG) as f:
    r=csv.reader(f); header=next(r)
    for line in r:
        if len(line)<6: continue
        try: ts=parse(line[0])
        except: continue
        mrows.append({'ts':ts,'agent_id':line[1],'brief_id':line[2],'kind':line[4],'desc':line[5]})
print("Manager rows (briefs):", len(mrows))

# index worker rows by agent_id, non-lifecycle = status not in lifecycle set
LIFECYCLE={'brief_start','brief_stop','baseline','status',''}
def first_work_after(agent, t):
    # agent_id in manager is the worker id (0..3)
    rows=sorted(wrows.get(int(agent),[]), key=lambda r:r['ts'])
    for rr in rows:
        if rr['ts']>=t and rr['status'] not in LIFECYCLE:
            return rr['ts']
    return None

handoffs=[]
slow=[]
for m in mrows:
    try:
        agent=int(m['agent_id'])
    except:
        continue
    if agent not in workers: continue
    fw=first_work_after(agent, m['ts'])
    if fw is None: continue
    gap=(fw-m['ts']).total_seconds()
    if gap<0: continue
    handoffs.append(gap)
    if gap>300:
        slow.append((m['ts'],agent,m['brief_id'],gap))
if handoffs:
    handoffs_sorted=sorted(handoffs)
    med=statistics.median(handoffs)
    p95=handoffs_sorted[int(0.95*len(handoffs_sorted))-1] if len(handoffs_sorted)>1 else handoffs_sorted[0]
    print(f"n={len(handoffs)} handoffs, median={med:.1f}s, p95={p95:.1f}s, max={max(handoffs):.1f}s, min={min(handoffs):.1f}s")
    print(f"Handoffs > 5min: {len(slow)}")
    for s in sorted(slow,key=lambda x:-x[3])[:15]:
        print(f"   brief at {s[0]} W{s[1]} brief-{s[2]} gap={s[3]/60:.1f}min")

# ---------- Respawn / death detection ----------
# Heuristic: brief_start rows whose brief_id repeats for a worker, or manager 'bookkeeping' stops.
print("\n=== DEATH/RESPAWN SIGNALS ===")
for w in workers:
    rows=sorted(wrows[w], key=lambda r:r['ts'])
    starts=[r for r in rows if r['status']=='brief_start']
    seen=Counter(s['brief_id'] for s in starts)
    dups={k:v for k,v in seen.items() if v>1}
    print(f"W{w}: brief_ids started more than once (respawn signal): {dups}")

print("\nDONE")

# Behavior Report — `2026-06-22-09-10-03-qr_v2`

*Single experiment, 4-worker `optimize-tree` run on one B200. 172 brief-branches
across workers W0/W1/W2/W3, 2026-06-22 09:16 → 2026-06-24 17:38 (≈56.4 h wall).*

## Executive Summary

This was a long, productive, and — given the conditions — strikingly reliable run.
Across 56.4 h of walltime the fleet logged 332 trials over 172 brief-branches
(83 of which produced ≥1 trial; the other 89 were write-only or instantly-abandoned
briefs). Sustained throughput was modest at ≈4.5 trials per active worker-hour, but
that number is set almost entirely by the cost of a single CUDA iteration on this
problem (build + validate-on-22-ranked-shapes + benchmark + nsys/ncu profile), not by
agent stalling. The headline reliability story is that the run survived **≈71 API-drop
worker deaths and ≈33 manager respawns** with zero lost work and **zero genuine
early-termination** — the manager recovered every crashed worker losslessly from its
branch + log, and a mid-run torch 2.11→2.12.1+cu130 venv upgrade plus an end-of-run
spin-down were both executed as clean, operator-directed pause/resume windows.

**Key takeaways**

- **The fleet is remarkably balanced, not bottlenecked on one worker.** Per-worker
  throughput is 4.67 / 4.47 / 4.55 / 3.89 trials/active-h for W0/W1/W2/W3 — every
  worker is within **0.86–1.04× of the fleet median**. There is *no* 2× outlier; the
  large per-*brief* variance (CoV 3.49×) comes from brief *length*, not worker skill.
- **The 4th worker arrived 39 h late.** W3 did not exist until 2026-06-24 00:27 — the
  run was a **3-worker fleet for its first ~39 h** and only reached 4 workers for the
  final ~17 h. Judged against the *intended* size per era, the fleet was at full
  strength **82.6 % of the 3-worker era and 79.2 % of the 4-worker era**.
- **Lock contention on the single GPU is a real, double-digit tax.** Only one of four
  workers can hold the exclusive `gpu-0` lock (bench/profile/validate) at a time;
  captured lock-wait totals **≈9.5 h ≈ 17 % of fleet walltime** (a conservative floor —
  truncated logs imply the true figure is higher), with the worst single wait
  **12.8 min**. This, not agent idleness, is the dominant structural drag on a 4-on-1
  fleet.
- **Worker deaths were frequent but invisible to the result.** ≈71 distinct
  API-mid-response deaths (W0:27, W1:21, W2:21, W3:2), heaviest on 06-22/06-23,
  each recovered by the manager re-reading the branch and re-issuing the in-flight
  brief. Several "deaths" were stale duplicate notifications the manager correctly
  declined to act on.
- **No agent tried to quit the run.** 34 messages are workers *correctly* declaring one
  brief exhausted and handing back to the manager (normal). The only halt-and-wait was
  W2 on brief-69 correctly honoring a *direct user freeze* over a conflicting
  coordinator instruction — the right call, not a give-up.

**One-line:** 172 branches · 332 trials · 56.4 h wall · mean ≈4.5 trials/active-worker-h
(worst sustained worker 3.89) · reliability verdict: **high** — frequent infrastructure
failures, zero work lost, zero spurious termination.

## Fleet Behavior

### Worker Concurrency Over Time

Active intervals were built by pairing each worker's `brief_start` with its next
`brief_stop`. Bucketed into 5-minute windows over the 56.4 h run:

| Active workers | Windows | Walltime | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (fully idle) | 13 | 1.08 h | 1.9 % |
| 1 | 9 | 0.75 h | 1.3 % |
| 2 | 68 | 5.67 h | 10.0 % |
| 3 | 423 | 35.25 h | 62.5 % |
| 4 (peak) | 164 | 13.67 h | 24.2 % |

Peak concurrency was **4**, but reached only in the final ~17 h: **worker W3's first
activity is 2026-06-24 00:27**, ~39 h into the run. So the raw "73.9 % under strength
vs. 4" figure is misleading — for most of the run the *target* was 3, not 4. Splitting
by era against the intended size:

- **3-worker era (start → 06-24 00:27, 39.25 h):** at full strength (≥3) **82.6 %**,
  under-strength **14.6 %**, fully idle **2.8 %**.
- **4-worker era (06-24 00:27 → end, 17.25 h):** at full strength (≥4) **79.2 %**,
  under-strength **20.8 %**, fully idle **0 %**.

The longest fully-idle stretch is small (the idle windows are scattered single buckets,
mostly clustered around the late-run maintenance/spin-down). The under-strength time is
the aggregate cost of the death/respawn churn — each death drops the fleet by one worker
until the manager notices and respawns (handoff median 82 s, below). The fleet never
collapsed; it ran one-worker-down briefly and often, not many-down for long.

### Brief-Cycle Timing (manager → worker handoff)

For each of the 206 manager-log brief rows, the handoff latency is the gap from the
manager writing the brief to the matching worker emitting `brief_start` for that
`brief_id`. Over the 170 briefs with a clean same-id match:

- **median 82 s, p95 616 s (~10 min), max 3103 s (51.7 min).**
- **16 briefs exceeded 5 min.** The 36 briefs without a clean same-id match are exactly
  the respawned/duplicated briefs (a crashed instance's brief_start does not line up
  with the re-issued row).

The slowest handoffs cluster on 06-23 when death churn peaked — e.g. W1 brief-23
(51.7 min, 06-23 10:10), W0 brief-19 (39.0 min, 06-23 05:24), W2 brief-69 (29.1 min,
06-24 14:50, during the late-run freeze). These long handoffs are the manager waiting on
a dead-worker respawn or on a busy GPU, not the worker ignoring a brief. *(Note: the
gap from `brief_start` to the worker's first logged trial is a separate ~20 min median —
that is one build+validate+benchmark cycle, i.e. the cost of doing the work, not a
handoff problem.)*

### Lock Contention

`autocuda run slice` (build, **shared** `build` lock) and `autocuda run exclusive`
(bench/profile/validate, **exclusive** `gpu-0` lock) emit paired acquire/release lines
in the session logs. De-duplicated across replayed sessions (871 unique acquisitions:
231 build/shared, 640 gpu-0/exclusive — all GPU locks are `gpu-0`, a single B200):

| Lock kind | Acquisitions | Total wait | Median wait | Max wait | Total hold (`ran`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `build` / shared (builds) | 231 | 2.61 h | 8.3 s | 447.5 s | 0.63 h |
| `gpu-0` / exclusive (bench/profile/validate) | 640 | 6.86 h | 0.0 s | **768.0 s** | 15.41 h |
| **Total** | 871 | **9.47 h** | — | 768.0 s | 16.0 h |

The GPU was held under exclusive lock **≈15.4 h ≈ 27 % of walltime** — that is the

The run's behavior is best summarized as **a slow-but-steady, infrastructure-stressed
fleet that never actually lost ground.** Sustained throughput sits at ≈4.5 trials per
active worker-hour and is essentially flat across W0/W1/W2 — the differences are noise.

discarded trial pays for a build, a validate over 22 ranked/ill-conditioned shapes, a
benchmark, and frequently an nsys/ncu profile, and the heavy shapes (n=2048/4096, B=640)

3.49× looks alarming until you see it is entirely a function of brief *length* —
25-second probes and 5.7-hour marathons share one column — and collapses to near-zero
once aggregated per worker. The variance is *not* driven by an outlier worker.

**Where did the time actually go?** Two places, both structural rather than behavioral.
First, the **exclusive GPU lock**: the single B200 was held under exclusive lock ≈15.4 h
(≈27 % of walltime) and the fleet paid ≈9.5 h (≈17 %, a floor) waiting to acquire it,
with a 12.8-min worst case. With four workers and one GPU this is unavoidable — three
workers idle whenever one benchmarks — and it is the clearest reason the gaps in
`Gaps And Stalls` line up with the heavy-shape, high-trial briefs (brief-44, brief-26,
brief-39, brief-52). Second, the **death/respawn churn**: ≈71 deaths cost the fleet its
under-strength time (14.6 % of the 3-worker era, 20.8 % of the 4-worker era) and stretched
the slowest manager→worker handoffs to 30–52 min on 06-23 when the manager was waiting on
respawns. Crucially, neither bottleneck is the agent stalling — the median handoff is
82 s and the fully-idle time is <2 % of the run.

The reliability engineering is the standout. A 56-hour run that absorbs ≈71 API-drop
deaths, a torch major-version venv swap, and a deliberate spin-down — all without losing
a single brief's work and without one spurious "should I stop?" — is the behavior you
want from an autonomous harness. The manager's lossless recovery (read branch + log,
re-issue brief), its restraint on stale death notifications, and its correct handling of
the venv window (drain → snapshot for rollback → upgrade on idle GPU → verify 22/22 →
resume) all held up. The one halt (W2/brief-69) was the agent *correctly* prioritizing a
direct user instruction over a conflicting relay — a feature, not a fault.

**Recommendations.**
1. **Attack the GPU lock, not the agent.** ≈17–27 % of walltime is GPU serialization on
   a 4-on-1 fleet. The highest-leverage next change is either fewer workers per GPU
   (3-on-1 showed 82.6 % full-strength vs. the 4-on-1 era's 79.2 %, at lower contention)
   or shorter benchmark/profile holds (cache profiles, profile fewer shapes per trial,
   or gate ncu behind a kept-result filter) so the exclusive lock is released sooner.
2. **Harden against API-drop deaths.** ≈71 deaths and ~33 respawns dominated the
   operational noise and pushed worst-case handoffs past 50 min. A faster death detector
   (tighter respawn polling) or automatic mid-response retry would reclaim most of the
   under-strength time without changing the optimization logic.
3. **Launch the full worker count from the start.** W3 arriving 39 h late means ~39 h of
   3-worker throughput where 4 were intended; spawning all workers at launch (and keeping
   the no-op-brief rate down — 89 of 172 briefs produced nothing) would raise effective
   fleet utilization on the next run.

66 of 172 branches recorded a gap (a >10 min quiet transition between trials), 154 gaps

## Early-Termination Attempts

**Zero genuine early-terminations.** No worker or the manager ever stopped to ask the
user whether to end the run. Breakdown of the patterns found in the session logs:

- **Genuine halt-and-wait: 1 event (W2, brief-69, 06-24 14:50/15:17).** W2 *correctly*

  "Just leave the branch as it is") conflicted with the coordinator-relayed brief. It held
  the branch frozen and asked the user to resolve the conflict — the harness-correct
  behavior (a coordinator's claim of user consent is not user consent), **not** a
  give-up.
- **Normal brief-exhaustion handoffs: 34.** Workers concluding *one brief* is mined out
  and returning control to the manager for a fresh brief (e.g. *"I've exhausted the
  brief's productive vein… before stopping"*). This is the designed `explore-brief`
  loop, not early termination. Several explicitly acknowledged the no-stopping mandate
  and probed one more lever before handing back.
- **Manager "looks converged" moments: 2, both continued.** The manager twice reasoned
  the search space was exhausted (06-22 20:16, 06-23 22:15 — the latter after a
  "completeness critic" subagent returned EXHAUSTED) yet kept the ≤1000 µs goal hook
  active and **did not stop**.

## Other Aberrant Behavior

- **Worker deaths from API-mid-response, ~71 distinct (W0:27, W1:21, W2:21, W3:2).** The
  defining operational fact of the run. Workers died mid-tool-use (losing their in-memory
  summary); the manager recovered each losslessly by reading the branch + worker log and
  re-issuing the in-flight brief via `autocuda init brief`. Clustered on 06-22 (early)
  and 06-23. Representative: *"Worker 0 died with an API error mid-response… 155 tool
  uses over ~58 min before dying… The summary is lost, so I need to read the worker log
  and git branch to recover."* (06-22 13:19).
- **~33 manager respawn actions (06-22:11, 06-23:20, 06-24:2)**, plus many *declined*
  respawns — the manager repeatedly recognized **stale duplicate death notifications**
  and correctly took "no action, no respawn" to avoid double-spawning a live worker. Good
  defensive behavior under a noisy failure signal.
- **Dangling-brief bookkeeping (manager-authored balancing `brief_stop` rows).** When a
  crashed instance left a `brief_start` with no `brief_stop`, the manager emitted a
  compensating stop so start/stop counts reconciled — e.g. W0 brief-4 (06-22 19:14). This
  is why worker logs show *more* stops than starts (W0 57 vs 54, W2 60 vs 55, etc.); it
  is correct bookkeeping, not a logging error, but it does mean raw start/stop counts
  must be paired carefully.
- **Duplicate brief_ids per worker (respawn fingerprints):** W0 restarted brief-44 **5×**,
  brief-4/23/48 2× each; W2 brief-18/39 2×; W3 brief-0/19 2×. Each duplicate is a death
  + respawn of the same in-flight brief, consistent with the death log.
- **Late fleet expansion.** W3 was added ~39 h in (first activity 06-24 00:27) rather
  than at launch — the run effectively changed its target worker count mid-stream. Worth
  flagging for any apples-to-apples throughput comparison with other runs.
- **89 zero-trial briefs.** Slightly over half of all briefs produced no trial. Most are
  manager briefs superseded by a redirect before a worker engaged, or picked up and
  abandoned at build time; a few coincide with a death between brief-write and first
  build. Not a correctness problem, but it inflates the branch count well above the
  number of *substantive* explorations (83).

## Analysis

The run's behavior is best summarized as **a slow-but-steady, infrastructure-stressed
fleet that never actually lost ground.** Sustained throughput sits at ≈4.5 trials per
active worker-hour and is essentially flat across W0/W1/W2 — the differences are noise.
That rate is governed by the per-iteration cost of this specific problem: every kept or
discarded trial pays for a build, a validate over 22 ranked/ill-conditioned shapes, a
benchmark, and frequently an nsys/ncu profile, and the heavy shapes (n=2048/4096, B=640)
make a single benchmark a tens-of-minutes affair. The per-*brief* trials/hour CoV of
3.49× looks alarming until you see it is entirely a function of brief *length* —
25-second probes and 5.7-hour marathons share one column — and collapses to near-zero
once aggregated per worker. The variance is *not* driven by an outlier worker.

**Where did the time actually go?** Two places, both structural rather than behavioral.
First, the **exclusive GPU lock**: the single B200 was held under exclusive lock ≈15.4 h
(≈27 % of walltime) and the fleet paid ≈9.5 h (≈17 %, a floor) waiting to acquire it,
with a 12.8-min worst case. With four workers and one GPU this is unavoidable — three
workers idle whenever one benchmarks — and it is the clearest reason the gaps in
`Gaps And Stalls` line up with the heavy-shape, high-trial briefs (brief-44, brief-26,
brief-39, brief-52). Second, the **death/respawn churn**: ≈71 deaths cost the fleet its
under-strength time (14.6 % of the 3-worker era, 20.8 % of the 4-worker era) and stretched
the slowest manager→worker handoffs to 30–52 min on 06-23 when the manager was waiting on
respawns. Crucially, neither bottleneck is the agent stalling — the median handoff is
82 s and the fully-idle time is <2 % of the run.

The reliability engineering is the standout. A 56-hour run that absorbs ≈71 API-drop
deaths, a torch major-version venv swap, and a deliberate spin-down — all without losing
a single brief's work and without one spurious "should I stop?" — is the behavior you
want from an autonomous harness. The manager's lossless recovery (read branch + log,
re-issue brief), its restraint on stale death notifications, and its correct handling of
the venv window (drain → snapshot for rollback → upgrade on idle GPU → verify 22/22 →
resume) all held up. The one halt (W2/brief-69) was the agent *correctly* prioritizing a
direct user instruction over a conflicting relay — a feature, not a fault.

**Recommendations.**
1. **Attack the GPU lock, not the agent.** ≈17–27 % of walltime is GPU serialization on
   a 4-on-1 fleet. The highest-leverage next change is either fewer workers per GPU
   (3-on-1 showed 82.6 % full-strength vs. the 4-on-1 era's 79.2 %, at lower contention)
   or shorter benchmark/profile holds (cache profiles, profile fewer shapes per trial,
   or gate ncu behind a kept-result filter) so the exclusive lock is released sooner.
2. **Harden against API-drop deaths.** ≈71 deaths and ~33 respawns dominated the
   operational noise and pushed worst-case handoffs past 50 min. A faster death detector
   (tighter respawn polling) or automatic mid-response retry would reclaim most of the
   under-strength time without changing the optimization logic.
3. **Launch the full worker count from the start.** W3 arriving 39 h late means ~39 h of
   3-worker throughput where 4 were intended; spawning all workers at launch (and keeping
   the no-op-brief rate down — 89 of 172 briefs produced nothing) would raise effective
   fleet utilization on the next run.
